summaries.title: Present Perfect vs Present Perfect Continuous

sections.heading: Both tenses link the past to NOW
paragraphs: PP = the RESULT · what is done
PPC = the ACTIVITY · how long

sections.heading: 1 · Present Perfect
paragraphs: have/has + V3

rows: Have you eaten? — Yes, I have.

sections.heading: Uses — linked to now · no finished time
rows: I've had three exams this week.
I've known Ziad for ten years.
He's scored two goals so far.
Your English has improved a lot.
the best book I've ever read

sections.heading: V3 not V2
paragraphs: ✗ has went ✓ has gone
✓ Yes, I have. ✗ Yes, I've.

sections.heading: 2 · Present Perfect Continuous
paragraphs: have/has + been + V-ing

rows: It has been raining all day.
How long have you been waiting?

sections.heading: Uses — focus on the activity and its duration
rows: 1. Started in the past, still going
He's been waiting for an hour.
It's wet. It has been raining.
I've been going to the gym lately.
Someone has been using my phone!

sections.heading: Typical signal words
items: How long…? · for · since · all day / all morning · lately · recently
Answer to How long…? → For twenty minutes. / Since 3 o'clock.
-ing spelling: write → writing · run → running · lie → lying · study → studying

sections.heading: “been” never changes
paragraphs: ✗ has being / be working · ✗ has been work

sections.heading: 3 · The Core Difference — Result vs Activity
paragraphs: How many? → PP | How long? → PPC

rows: I've cleaned my room. Now it's tidy.
I've been cleaning my room. That's why I'm tired.
Karim has read the book. (page 300 of 300)
Karim has been reading the book. (page 120 of 300)
He has been writing emails all morning.
Someone has eaten my sandwich! (plate empty)
Someone has been eating my sandwich! (half missing)

sections.heading: Both fine
paragraphs: live, work, study, teach + for/since: I've worked / I've been working here for five years. (PPC can sound more temporary)

sections.heading: ★ Exam Tricks
paragraphs: The shortcuts that decide multiple-choice answers

sections.heading: Trick 1 · Finished time → Past Simple, not PP
paragraphs: yesterday · …ago · last… · in 2019 · When…?
✗ I have seen him yesterday. ✓ I saw him…
✗ When have you left? ✓ When did you leave?

sections.heading: Trick 2 · Number / quantity → PP, never PPC
paragraphs: three · twice · How many? · all the cake
✓ I've drunk four cups of coffee today.
✗ I've been drinking four cups today.

sections.heading: Trick 3 · How long? + action verb → PPC
paragraphs: How long have you been waiting?
Stative → PP: How long have you known him?
How many? → PP: How many have you sold?

sections.heading: Trick 4 · Visible evidence → PPC
paragraphs: tired · wet · dirty · red eyes · out of breath
The grass is wet. It has been raining.

sections.heading: Trick 5 · Stative verb → no -ing, even with for/since
paragraphs: ✗ I've been knowing him for years.
✓ I've known him for years.

sections.heading: Trick 6 · One short action + result now → PP
paragraphs: I've lost my keys, so I can't get in.
“I've been losing my keys” = again and again

sections.heading: Trick 7 · been + V-ing = active · been + V3 = passive
paragraphs: He has been cleaning the room. (he does it)
The room has been cleaned. (it can't clean itself)

sections.heading: Trick 8 · “This morning” — is it still morning?
paragraphs: (10 a.m.) I've sent five emails this morning.
(4 p.m.) I sent five emails this morning.

sections.heading: Trick 9 · for + a finished period → Past Simple
paragraphs: He worked in Kuwait for five years. (back now)
He has worked there for five years. (still there)

sections.heading: Trick 10 · It's the first time… → PP
paragraphs: ✗ It's the first time I see snow.
✓ It's the first time I've seen snow.

sections.heading: Trick 11 · Up to now + for/since → not a present tense
paragraphs: ✗ I know him for years. ✓ I've known him…
✗ I'm waiting for an hour. ✓ I've been waiting…

sections.heading: Trick 12 · Didn't happen at all → usually PP
paragraphs: I haven't eaten anything since breakfast.
I haven't seen Omar for months.

sections.heading: Trick 13 · he's = he has or he is?
paragraphs: + V3 / been = has: He's gone. He's been working.
+ V-ing / adjective = is: He's going out.

sections.heading: Trick 14 · Life over / chance gone → Past Simple
paragraphs: Einstein won the Nobel Prize. ✗ has won
Have you seen the exhibition? (still open → PP)

sections.heading: Trick 15 · Signal-word errors
paragraphs: ✗ I haven't never · ✗ I have ever been to Paris
✓ I've never… · ✓ I haven't finished yet.

sections.heading: Decision map: ask in order
paragraphs: 1. Finished time word? → PAST SIMPLE
2. Stative verb? → PP
3. Number / done result? → PP
4. Duration / evidence? → PPC
5. ever, just, already, yet… → PP (usually)

sections.heading: 4 · Signal Words & Position

rows: We've won two games so far.

sections.heading: Mid position
paragraphs: have/has + already · just · ever · never · recently + V3

sections.heading: 5 · Since · For · Been · Gone

rows: 2020 · Monday · 8 o'clock · last week · yesterday · I was a child
six years · two hours · a week · ages · the last two years

paragraphs: Test: “From when?” → since · “How much time?” → for
✗ since two years · ✗ for 2019 · ✗ since a week
since + clause → usually Past Simple: I've known him since we were kids.

rows: Dad has gone to work. (not here)

sections.heading: 6 · Stative Verbs — No -ing

rows: like, love, hate, prefer, want, need

sections.heading: Action meaning → -ing is OK
Exception
paragraphs: Informal speech may say I've been wanting to… — in exams, stative = no -ing.

sections.heading: 7 · Key Transformations
paragraphs: …ago → for · in/on/at → since · the last time → haven't … since

rows: I started learning French two years ago.
I've been learning French for two years.
The last time I saw Karim was in June.
I haven't seen Karim since June.
It's three years since I saw him.
I haven't seen him for three years.
This is my first visit to Luxor.
I bought this phone two years ago. (still mine)
I've had this phone for two years.
I've never seen such a big fish.
It's the biggest fish I've ever seen.

remember: Context decides — these are strong exam patterns, not unbreakable laws.
PP = Present Perfect · PPC = Present Perfect Continuous · PS = Past Simple
